archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A conservative, timing-and-checkdown passer who keeps the ball short and on schedule, and who only works when the run game and defense carry the load and he avoids giving the ball away.

report.headline: Two ugly September outings cost him the job; now he's Atlanta's emergency third quarterback
report.take:
Cooper Rush has always been a fill-in who wins by not losing: short throws, few sacks and enough completions to let the offense lean on its run game. That version of him never showed up in 2026. He started Week 1 at Pittsburgh, came on for 58% of the snaps in Week 2 against Carolina after Tua Tagovailoa started, and Michael Penix Jr. has started every game since. As of the latest depth chart Rush is QB3. Read his line as a closed two-game file, not a running season.

That file is about as bad as a quarterback line gets. His -0.635 EPA per dropback ranks 48th of 49, his -13.61 CPOE is 47th, and his 10.3% interception rate is dead last. The damage has a shape. Throws under 10 air yards were only mildly negative (-0.203 EPA, 63.3% completions). The nine throws at 10+ yards produced three interceptions and -13.2 EPA, which is most of the hole. He also took sacks on 62.5% of his pressured dropbacks, last among qualifiers, behind a line whose hit rate allowed ranks first in the league. Those sacks were largely his own doing.

The numbers hide two things. First, the sample is tiny, and the career says this isn't exactly who he is. His pressure-to-sack rate ranked 4th in 2022 and 2nd in 2025, and his interception counts were modest in his longer Dallas stints. Second, the season tells you plainly what he isn't. His intended air yards fell to 5.34 and his aggressiveness to 7.69%, after an aDOT of 7.1 and aggressiveness near 20% in 2024. When he did push the ball into the intermediate middle, he was inaccurate (23.1% bad throws) and late. A 33-year-old backup whose accuracy has been below expected in every charted season doesn't have a lot of margin when the safe throws also stop working.

Where it's heading: nowhere, unless two quarterbacks ahead of him go down. Atlanta is a run-first team (pass rate over expected -6.5, 28th) with the 5th-best rushing EPA. That is the right environment for a caretaker, so an emergency appearance would look like checkdowns and handoffs, not a revival.

strengths.title: Underneath and left-side throws held up
strengths.body: The quick, short throws that are his whole game were roughly break-even: near-zero EPA with a 50% success rate from 0-9 air yards. Throws to the left were genuinely good, at +0.482 EPA with 83.3% completions. That fits a decade-long profile of a timing passer who can run the simple part of an offense. It is the floor that would remain in any emergency spot, though the samples are 12 to 16 throws.

strengths.title: Historically he doesn't take sacks
strengths.body: His 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate this year is badly out of character. He ranked 2nd in 2025 and 4th in 2022 at turning pressure into something other than a sack. Five sacks across two games is too small a sample to overwrite years of evidence. Behind a line that allows the fewest hits in the league, that should normalize if he plays again.

strengths.title: Found Drake London when he looked
strengths.body: London was the one target who added value with Rush throwing (+0.447 EPA per target on nine looks). Every other regular target was negative. It says the plays that worked were simple throws to his best receiver, which is what a backup is supposed to do.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws turned into turnovers
concerns.body: Three of his four interceptions came on seven throws at 10-19 air yards, a -12.2 EPA cluster that sank his season on its own. Rush has never had the arm or accuracy to live in that window. His CPOE has been below expected in every charted season, and his bad-throw rate jumped from 17.3% last year. Some of the interception rate is small-sample bad luck, but the inaccuracy is real.

concerns.title: Couldn't move the chains on third down
concerns.body: He converted 15.4% of third downs at an average of 8.5 yards to go, with three sacks and a -36.1 CPOE there. Long third downs are where a checkdown passer's limits show most. Atlanta's offense is built to avoid those situations, but he kept landing in them.

concerns.title: Checkdowns to the back went nowhere
concerns.body: Bijan Robinson drew a team-high 14 targets at -0.475 EPA each, and throws behind the line of scrimmage ran at -0.422 EPA. For a game manager, the screen and checkdown game is supposed to be the safe base. Here it was a drain, partly because he was short of the sticks by more than five yards on average.

trend.note: Week 2 was worse than Week 1: CPOE went from -10.4 to -16.8 and bad throws from 19% to 29.4%, in a 3-34 home loss. Penix has started every game since Week 3, and Rush has slid to third on the depth chart.

nextGame.headline: QB3 against Kansas City; he shouldn't see the field
nextGame.body:
Rush isn't expected to play. Penix has started seven straight games, and Rush sits behind both him and Tagovailoa. If he were forced in, Kansas City is a bad fit for him. The Chiefs allow -0.115 EPA on short passes (4th) and have held opposing WR1s to -0.1 EPA per target (2nd), which takes away his only working area: quick, short throws to his top receiver. Their soft spot is deep passing (21st), and he doesn't throw deep. The one break is that they barely pressure anyone (sack rate 31st, hit rate 27th), which would blunt his sack problem.

On Kansas City's side, Patrick Mahomes is questionable with an elbow strain, and corners Mansoor Delane (out) and L'Jarius Sneed (IR) are missing. That thins the secondary for whoever plays quarterback for Atlanta. Atlanta's own injuries, a backup back on IR and a rotational receiver out, don't change much for a third-string passer.

keyMatchups.title: Stingy short-area defense versus a checkdown passer
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City ranks 4th against short throws, the exact zone where Rush's season was least bad. A quarterback averaging 5.34 intended air yards has nowhere else to go against that.

keyMatchups.title: Weak Chiefs pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City's sack rate ranks 31st, so a relief appearance would likely come with a cleaner pocket than he had in September. That would test whether his 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate was noise.

keyMatchups.title: Depth chart, not matchup, decides it
keyMatchups.body: Penix has started every game since Week 3, and Rush is listed third. Barring injuries to two quarterbacks, the matchup is academic.

nextGame.watch: Whether Rush is even active on game day: any snaps would mean something went badly wrong with Penix or Tagovailoa.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect near-zero involvement. Rush's two-game line, and the 34-interception pace17 it produces, says more about how bad a small sample can look than about what he'd do over a real stretch. His history points to a low-sack, low-aDOT backup whose accuracy sits below expected. If he played again, the interception rate should fall sharply and the sack rate should drift back toward his career norms, especially behind a line this good at keeping quarterbacks clean.

What won't change is the ceiling. He doesn't push the ball downfield, Atlanta passes far less than the situation predicts, and his completion rate over expected has been negative every year. In an emergency start, the realistic version is 110-180 passing yards with a touchdown or a turnover deciding the grade. Week to week, the projection is essentially nothing.

projections.stat: Passing yards in an emergency start

swingFactors: Injuries to both Penix and Tagovailoa
Whether his career-norm sack avoidance returns

confidence.note: Role is clear (QB3); the stats rest on only 46 dropbacks.
